extracted.intended_audience: university educators, administrators, policymakers, and readers interested in the philosophy of higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and standards about the purpose, character, and desirable outcomes of a university (liberal) education as argued in an academic discourse. Focuses on what counts as a good university education and how it relates to professional life and religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual culture as an end in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: “Intellectual culture is its own end; for what has its end in itself, has its use in itself also.” Education whose end is the cultivation of the intellect is therefore good in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and analogy: as bodily health is a good in itself and yet also useful, so cultivated intellect is intrinsically valuable and thereby necessarily useful. This principle undercuts the objection that education must point to a temporal calling to be 'useful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The good (liberal) is necessarily useful
rubrics_metrics.description: “Though the useful is not always good, the good is always useful.” A good (i.e., excellent) intellectual state will overflow and produce benefits beyond itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that excellence in the intellect diffuses 'good' to the possessor and to society; usefulness here is not mechanical or vocational but the reproduction and dissemination of good qualities (admiration, desire, gratitude) and social benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal education = cultivation of the intellect (not professional training)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Liberal Education consists in the culture of the intellect rather than being primarily 'professional' or vocational training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes University function from purely professional instruction: a University teaches 'all knowledge' by teaching branches of knowledge and gives a survey and philosophical standpoint that preserves breadth and prevents absorption into a narrow professional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of the understanding: speculation, original inquiry, and first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should cultivate 'a talent for speculation and original inquiry,' and 'the invaluable habit of pushing things up to their first principles,' as well as the ability to collect dry facts as materials for reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with over-cultivation of imagination or mere elegant taste; the aim is to form the 'solid and masculine parts of the understanding' and to avoid training that leaves students unable or unwilling to defend opinions or prove assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as the form of knowledge: mastery as system
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge pursued for its own sake must be mastered and appropriated 'as a system consisting of parts, related one to the other, and interpretative of one another in the unity of a whole' — i.e., 'Philosophy must be its form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises active, synthetic understanding rather than passive acquisition; education should produce comprehension of relations among parts of knowledge and an 'illumination' or location of things within a coherent intellectual map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of sound judgment (exactness and vigour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central educational aim is to form the power of judgment — 'the master-principle' that gives strength in any subject and enables one to 'seize the strong point' — with the habits of exactness and vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment is developed not by narrow rote learning but by varied reading, discipline, and observation; the enlargement of intellectual circle increases judgment; judgment 'lives' by comparison and discrimination and requires a diverse assemblage of studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and variety of studies (mutual correction and complement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A course of diversified reading — history, eloquence, poetry, ethics, theories of speculation, the fine arts, etc. — is necessary because these disciplines 'conspire in an union of effect' and mutually correct each other's defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific benefits: history gives fulness, moral philosophy strength, and poetry elevation. Combined studies produce a richer vein of thought than any single discipline and prevent the faults of confined reading (flashiness, jejuneness, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities cultivate faculties that enable professional success
rubrics_metrics.description: While not primarily vocational, liberal education subserves professional education by cultivating faculties (judgment, reasoning, discrimination) that give a person the command of knowledge and adaptability across careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man of improved faculties can take up any science or calling with ease and success; cultivation precedes specialization and is the chief ingredient for professional ability rather than mere accumulation of technical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of over-specialization and mitigation of division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Though division of labour improves arts, an exclusive absorption in one employment 'degrades' the individual; university education should modify and restrain excessive specialisation by promoting liberal intercourse and common cultural ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Dr. Copleston: extreme concentration produces national wealth but contracts mental powers and habits; universities supply the 'common link' (literature) that unites different professions and checks narrow prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of social and civic virtues (fitness for the world)
rubrics_metrics.description: A University course's practical end is to 'train good members of society' — raising intellectual tone, purifying national taste, supplying true principles to popular enthusiasm, facilitating political power, and refining private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes concrete social competencies produced by liberal education: clear view of one's opinions, eloquence, force in urging views, ability to see things as they are, disentangle sophistry, converse and listen appropriately, influence and accommodate others, and perform public and private duties with grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should not be measured solely by subservience to a calling
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejects the maxim that the value of every attainment is to be measured solely by its subserviency to a future calling; warns against shaping the whole person 'in the exact mould of his technical character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that professional character is not the only role a person has; liberal accomplishments (e.g., speaking good sense in English) matter for social life, leisure, and the circulation of taste and opinion, and should be encouraged even if not directly remunerative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of cultivated reason to religion (Religion of Civilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The educated mind forms a 'Religion of Civilization' or a 'Religion of Reason' which may cooperate with, defend, or sometimes disturb revealed religion (here discussed in relation to Catholicism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes two senses: Reason rightly exercised leads to Catholic Faith, but Reason as an operative historical principle may construct its own religion, sometimes aligning and sometimes diverging from revealed truth; the discussion treats Catholicism chiefly as a pastoral moral system rather than creedal propositions.
